utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. I would like to greet everyone here in this courtroom, Mr. Scott, the Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else in the courtroom. We are starting late. I don't know for what reason. I was told that the Popovic Trial Chamber was late in finishing. I saw on my screen that Mr. Karnavas was in another case. So I don't exactly know what this delay is about. In any case, we are 20 minutes late, and we'll try to make up for it but I will first like to ask the registrar to give us some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you again, Your Honour. OTP has submitted a list of documents which should be tendered through a Mr. Rudy Gerritsen. This list will become Exhibit IC 591 under seal. In addition, several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness BH. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 592 under seal. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 593 while the list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 594 under seal. That's everything, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We are now going to move into private session for a few minutes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had asked for closed session but only out of great caution, Your Honour. There is -- there is a motion current -- perhaps it's safer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understood that Your Honour. I understand that. I was just wondering whether in the circumstance I could safely proceed but I think not actually, Your Honour. I -- may we go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reason we selected four and a half hours is for a reason and we think that that's a reasonable estimate of time that will be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do wish to raise a concern here, Your Honour. Here we are right before the witness testifies and we find out for the very first time that the Trial Chamber, on its own, has decided to make cuts and changes to the allocation of the time. The Prosecution obviously indicated it needed for its case four and a half hours. You cut their time and then you cut the Defence's time without recognising the amount of time that the Defence needs and I must -- I must say that again this is not the proper way to proceed. I've said it in the past; I'll say it again. This is not a way to ensure that the accused are getting a fair trial. And so -- and I certainly don't want the Prosecution at the end of their three hours to then try to introduce documents later on because they didn't have enough time to put it in. Of course, that's something that they feel compelled to do but it puts the Defence at a disadvantage and we're getting closer and closer to violating the Statute. We're getting to the point where there's no need for us to appear in Court if that's the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please stand. Can you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm Bo Pellnas, born on the 22nd of October, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a retired brigadier general from the Swedish armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you ever testified before a Tribunal on the events that took place in the former Yugoslavia or is this the first time you've testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm now going to ask you to read the solemn declaration shown to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You may sit down. It's the first time you've testified here, so let me give you a few words of explanation about this week of hearing where we will hear your testimony. In the first stage you will answer questions put to you by the Prosecutor. I'm sure you've met him before the hearing. The Prosecutor will also show you a number of documents that you've probably been shown earlier during the meeting you had with the Prosecution. Afterwards, the Defence counsel, who are sitting on your left, or as the case may be the accused themselves, may be able to put questions to you as part of the procedure we call the cross-examination. The four Judges sitting before you may, according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, may ask you questions at any time, but for practical purposes and so as not to obstruct the examination conducted by each of the parties, we find it better to put questions at the end. For extraordinary reasons, for example, because you're dealing with a particular document, we may decide to ask questions to deal with that particular document so as not to have to go back to it at the end. But usually we prefer to wait until the end to put questions to you. If you do not understand one of the questions put to you, do not hesitate to ask the person asking the question to repeat it. Please try to be extremely accurate when answering the questions. This is an oral proceedings, and what is important is what you will tell us and what will be confirmed and corroborated by documents that will be submitted to you. That's why you have a screen in front of you where what's being said by everyone here in this courtroom is transcribed. We have breaks every 90 minutes for technical reasons and also to give the witness the opportunity to rest, but if in the meantime you feel that you need to rest, do not hesitate to notify us and ask for a break. The Trial Chamber is ready to answer any questions you might have during the hearing. These are a few words of explanation about the way we are going to proceed today and on Wednesday and Thursday during this week that is entirely dedicated to you. Mr. Scott, without further ado and without wasting any more time because time is precious, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pellnas, good afternoon. General, our time under any scenario would be rather limited so I would like to go through some of your background fairly quickly. If you can just confirm a few facts for us, please. As you've just indicated, you are a retired senior officer from the Swedish armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You are an infantry or were an infantry officer by training. You began your military service in 1958. You were commissioned in 1961. You became a colonel in 1984 and brigadier general in 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During your time in the Swedish armed forces you were also a regimental or brigade commander. At a time you were in charge of what was called training and economy during the period from 1990 into 1992. Perhaps you could just briefly explain what that position involved.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was charged with the planning of the training of our conscripts and our units, and also to oversee the economy for this training as well as the housing for the training units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say to oversee the economy, might we understand that to be involved with administering the budget with these functions?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. Yes. At the time about 8 million Swedish crowns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was yours -- its correct that was your last assignment in Swedish armed forces?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, before leaving for the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During this same time period, at various parts of the time that I've just very quickly covered, is it correct, sir, that you were a United Nations battalion commander in Cyprus --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- during the period 1983, 1984?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you in charge of military observers in Kabul, Afghanistan during 1988, 1989?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that from approximately the 8th of November, 1992 until the 15th of November, 1993, you were the chief military observer for the United Nations Protection Force, or UNPROFOR, in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And of course it is that particular function which we will focus on in particular today. Your office in that function, your regular office was located in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In November 1993, you went to Geneva where you worked as military advisor to Thorvald Stoltenberg at the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you stayed in that position until approximately January 1995?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And one other item before finishing with the background. After being the chief military observer for the former Yugoslavia, you -- on the 14th of September, 1994, you went to Belgrade where you took charge of the border mission in Serbia-Montenegro at the Bosnia-Herzegovina border; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct based on what you told us a moment ago when you returned to the Swedish army, essentially, you completed these duties and most recently at that time your duty with Ambassador Stoltenberg, you returned to the Swedish army and retired from the armed forces and retired on the 15th of January, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: On the 1st of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 1st of February. Yes. Thank you very much. Just by way of additional background sir, it may come up in the course of your testimony, you wrote a book about your experience in the former Yugoslavia called, if I understand correctly, "Never ending"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: "Without end?"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that that book was primarily written in the summer of 1994 and published in February 1995?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was written during vacation in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then go directly to your position as chief UN military observer. Can you tell the Judges and the Judges have heard a bit about some of these different functions and have had witnesses who were themselves, at least one if not more, but I know at least one who was a UN military observer, in fact, but can you tell them a bit more about where the UN military observers failed you, what function they performed as part of the overall international involvement in the former Yugoslavia. For instance, how did they compare or relate to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think we had about 270, or something like that, observers when I started and they work in teams and the idea is to put them together from different nations and I think the idea behind that is to certify that they will be reporting objectively and not playing any national agendas and we had over 570 observers when I left UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And these observers, is it correct, were stationed throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. We had about, when I started, 60 observers in Sarajevo, and there were observers in Tuzla, in the Mostar region, in Dubrovnik, also I think in Bihac and of course in what was at the time known as Krajina, in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Could I ask that the witness be provided the binder of exhibits that will be used with the witness, please. Sir, what's just been placed in front of you is a binder full of exhibits which should all be tabbed in numerical order. So in the course of your testimony, I will be referring you to exhibits by number, and hopefully you will be able to find them there without too much trouble. Can I ask you please to go first of all to Exhibit 487. For the record, P 00487. They're not in the order in which we will necessarily use them, but they should be in numerical order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we don't have that exhibit, 487.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a 485.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe I've written down the number incorrectly. Excuse me, Your Honour. I apologise for that. Let me see if I can ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I apologise. There's been some error in that regard. Maybe we can come back to it in the course of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We'll need to share with the Bench our copy. I don't believe it's marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If it's in e-court, perhaps we could proceed in e-court, Your Honour. It would be easier to do it now than to obviously come back to it at some other time in the future especially with the time being limited. I apologise for whatever happened, but if I could have the assistance of the ushers to go to Exhibit P 00487 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, General, what will happen in this instance, I think it will come up on your computer screen, but apparently we don't have a hard copy. Sir, if you could just -- and with the assistance of the registry or usher if necessary, if you could just look at that document. I had shown you that previous -- previously. This is a document that's titled "Concept for the deployment of UNMO in Bosnia-Herzegovina command." And is this document, and if you need to -- if you need to go through more parts of the document I'll ask that the usher assist us in doing so, but is this a document that sets out essentially what you understood the structure of the UN military observers was during the time that you were the chief of that organisation, roughly speaking? It may not be exactly in detail, but primarily.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to assist us by going to item number 9 on the second page. And I'll abbreviate my questions in light of the fact that we don't have a hard copy. In item number 9, if you have that, you see that it indicates the nature of the task of UNMOs being, "A, patrolling in the area of responsibility; B, liaison with concerned parties; C, negotiations with authorities as required; D, inevitable/ad hoc humanitarian tasks." Do you find that to be an accurate statement of the various tasks or missions of the UNMOs during this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. If it is understood that reporting is imbedded in all of these tasks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I'm not sure that we need to look -- turn to the page but down below on the screen that we're looking at now you can see in fact that at that particular time there are approximately 19 observers allocated to Mostar in section 10. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as part of this document and again I don't think we necessarily have to go to it but there is an organisational chart which shows in fact one of the locations being Mostar. Could you briefly tell us what the reporting in fact -- you just mentioned the element or component of reporting. What was the arrangements or the structure or process for reporting from the UNMOs in the field to others that were in -- either to you or others who were along the chain of reporting or command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, their first reporting line was the operational line to the battalion commander which they -- in which whose area they were operating, and to the -- and for him to the headquarter. But they also through their line of -- I should say observer line of order reported directly to me in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So there was essentially a dual system of reporting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was actually quite deliberate the dual system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any particular terminology for what you called the -- the basic daily report that would be received from the field?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was called situation reports which came every morning, and I actually had three situation reports, one first put up by my headquarters and all the reports coming in from the observers. Secondly, there was the UNPROFOR sitrep, and I think also most of the time we had sitreps from the ECMM monitors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just briefly ask you about some of your travels and missions in the former Yugoslavia, again just by way of additional background. Is it correct, sir, that in the course of your duties in the former Yugoslavia you travelled to such places as Zvornik, Tuzla, Kiseljak, Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You travelled in the Tuzla, Vares, Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You travelled, I take it, in the Mostar, Metkovic area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Also Dubrovnik, Gorazde, Srebrenica --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about some of the senior officials or personalities that you interacted with during this time. You were stationed in -- or headquartered, if you will, in Zagreb. Did you ever have occasion to deal directly with the president of Croatia at that time, Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges approximately, and we'll just dealing with an approximation here, how many times that you had dealings or meetings with President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I would guess about four times directly. Three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: These primarily occurred - I can just look at my notes as well - all during 1993, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One was dealing with the Maslenica bridge problem. I was also taking part in a meeting at Brioni together with Ambassador Vollebaek and Gert Ahrends, and I was on another later meeting together with General Eide and Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you similar questions concerning the Croatian minister of defence Gojko Susak. Did you ever have occasion to meet with or have dealings with Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. When I took the office I had a number of meetings with him. We were at that time working with the Prevlaka peninsula and that problem, and I had rather good access to him in the beginning. After my period in Mostar in April 1993, he stopped seeing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know why he stopped seeing you in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think there might have been two reasons. I was too low ranking, actually, for him to associate with and, secondly, I think he found me a bit troublesome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Troublesome in what way, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: That's a good question. I don't know why he found me troublesome, actually. He should not have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Might I just point out for the record that the gentleman is mere speculating.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he stopped receiving me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, stop seeing him is one thing but speculating as to why he stopped seeing him unless he can verify the reasons is still speculation and we're dealing with facts, not speculation or fancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the times that you were at a meeting with Mr. Susak, can you characterise, can you tell the Chamber your observations of Mr. Susak in terms of his leadership, the way he participated in meetings, any observations that you can share with the Judges about --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. He was a very sharp personality. He was very determined. And the deals we made he kept them. So you could trust his word actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: And I think he had a great influence on the Croatian politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did that influence, to your knowledge or observation, extend beyond the borders of Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was generally said and generally known at the time that he had good contacts in the Herceg-Bosna region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever directly observe or participate in meetings where Mr. Susak was present along with perhaps various leaders, either military or political leaders from as you've just described it Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having put -- having put Mr. Susak on the table, if you will, and having asked you about your meetings or involvements with President Tudjman, can you share with the Chamber any observations about the interactions of President Tudjman or Mr. Susak in the course of any meetings that you observed where they dealt with each other?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I never met Susak together with President Tudjman at the same occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever have any dealings with General Bobetko, the head or chief officer of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Approximately how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: On two or three occasions. One major when we discussed the Prevlaka peninsula, late December 1992. Then there were more social visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what -- what was your experience in dealing with General Bobetko?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I found him very determined nationalist, of course, and besides that I don't have very much judgement to make about him. I met him so few times.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the -- during the occasions you did meet with him, were these in the context of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did you find him as a negotiator?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: We didn't cover much ground. There was an agreement about the peninsula, Prevlaka, signed by the Serbs. Zivota Panic, I think, signed it in Geneva. The Croats never signed it, and they left the agreement. And I tried to push him back into it, and I wasn't very successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, moving forward, to the period of February, March of 1993. Did you become involved in any meetings at the Sarajevo airport around that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I went there with Wahlgren, if I remember correctly, the general Swedish force commander and had a meeting personally with Ratko Mladic about bringing observers into Gorazde, if that is the occasion you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the same period of meetings at the Sarajevo airport, did you understand that General -- I'll try to follow your pronunciation, Wahlgren, was he also involved in other meetings around that time with various military leaders?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, there was a cease-fire negotiating taking part at the same occasion with General Petkovic, Mladic, and Halilovic, I believe it was. And there was a document signed of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing then -- moving on to April of 1993, did you become involved at that time in various efforts, peace-making efforts that led to your going to Mostar around the 18th of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't know so much about the background. There must have been something with the Vance Owen team working, but I was called up to Wahlgren one day and there was Ejup Ganic, the vice-president of Bosnia, and he asks Wahlgren to provide him with a high-ranking officer to go to Mostar to help to establish peaceful conditions, and he claimed that there was an agreement between himself and Mate -- yeah, Boban, Mate Boban. And Wahlgren pointed me to go, to follow him up to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just stop sir, and ask you because you've mentioned this name a couple of times. It may be a name that people in the courtroom are less familiar with than some of the others. General Wahlgren, what was his position at this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was force commander. And this was before there was a Special Representative of Secretary-General. So he had the full responsibility for the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say the entire mission, are you talking about all of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: All of UNPROFOR, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. So General Wahlgren, as I understand it, called you into a meeting with Mr. Ganic about trying -- he wanted someone to go to Mostar to meet with Mr. Boban and others?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I went to see Boban at the -- to make sure that they really had this agreement, and at that meeting he claimed that he also wanted -- they had agreed to create peaceful conditions in Mostar. And then I went back and had a meeting with Ejup Ganic, and we later left for Mostar. We flew to Split, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we get to that, let me go back and go a bit slower over a couple of items. You've just mentioned a meeting with General Wahlgren and Mr. Ganic as one. That was in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you meet with Mr. Boban in Zagreb later that same day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, at the Intercont [sic] Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you met with Mr. Ganic, you say, if I understood you, you met with Mr. Ganic again. Was that again later that same day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. We met him I think at the Hotel Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if you travelled to, in fact, then from Zagreb to Split to Medjugorje, that was on the 18th of April, 1993. Can we then understand that these other three meetings all took place on the 17th of --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going to your meeting with Mr. Boban, can you tell us, please, how -- how did that meeting -- how was it arranged? Where did you meet him and what conversation did you have?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I met him down in the lobby of the Intercontinental Hotel, and he explored some ideas he had about the future of Herceg-Bosna or Bosnia, but I didn't at the moment understand it so clearly. I understood it better when I met him in the Mostar region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you recall the positions or the things that Mr. Boban told you when you met him at the Intercontinental Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He indicated, as I remember it, that there should be a division of command between the Croats and the Muslims, and he was willing, he said, to hand over the command of the Croatian forces north of Kiseljak-Vares line to the Muslim forces, but he then demanded that all Muslim forces should be put under Croatian command south of that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when you say a line, did he indicate a line -- did he draw a line for you or give any --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Not on this occasion but later on he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this was a line roughly between Kiseljak and Vares?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah, roughly. Including, I think, the two enclaves south of the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any reaction at that time on this first occasion whether that -- that proposed division would have been acceptable to the BiH government or the Muslim party, if you will, at that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, not at all. And I don't think I fully understood what he told me at that first occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why do you say that this would not have been acceptable, as you, say not at all?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I meant I did -- I did not have any conversation with the BH authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At that time.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that you travelled then to Mostar on the 18th or to the -- well, ultimately perhaps Mostar, but to Medjugorje. Did you go -- did you enter into a meeting that was already in progress when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. To my -- I was astonished. The meeting had already started and it was led by the ECMM ambassador, Thebault, and so we -- they had to start it once again over again when we entered into the localities, which I believe was the hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you travelled from Zagreb that day and arrived in the meeting, Mr. Ganic was also travelling with you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. We flew to Split and the Spanish Battalion took us to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us briefly please, when you arrived at the meeting, other than the fact that it had already started, can you tell us who you saw at that meeting? And for now I'll just say at any part of that meeting, whether they were there at the beginning or any time during the course of the meeting, but who did you see participating in any part of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Mr. Jadranko Prlic was there. General Petkovic was there. The Muslim General Pasalic was there. I had believed until recently that the minister of defence, Stojic, was there, but obviously he arrived while I was out talking to General Petkovic. So he was not present probably when the meeting started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And anyone else that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, of course Thebault, the ambassador, and Ganic, myself, my adjutant, and probably General Lasic. I don't remember quite certain, but I think he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this Lasic was, just so -- for the record, that was Miljenko Lasic who was an HVO commander in the Mostar area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go back a little bit through the names that you've just mentioned. The first name you mentioned, if I'm not mistaken, is Jadranko Prlic was there. What did you know about Mr. Prlic at that time, about his position, anything that you knew at that time or observed or learned on that day about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could just have non-compound questions. The question becomes much more compound as Mr. Scott asks it. So what did he know beforehand would be one question. What did he learn that day, what did he learn thereafter. I would prefer having it that way. That way it would assist us in having a clear record and also for cross-examination purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just restate the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you know about Mr. Prlic when you arrived at the meeting that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I know that he was uphelding the function of so-called Prime Minister of Herceg-Bosna, and the president was Mate Boban. I might have had lunch with him in Mostar before this date but I can't really recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you had any meetings or dealings with Mr. Prlic after this meeting on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I only ran into him in Medjugorje in 1994 at the hotel Ana Marija. He sat together with some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps we're getting a bit ahead of ourselves, but what position or title did Mr. Prlic hold if you recall the second time you met him in 1994?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I can't really tell. I anticipated -- I pass on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in any event. You've also mentioned that Mr. Petkovic, General Petkovic was one of the persons in attendance. Is that the first time you had met General Petkovic or had you had any dealings with him before?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, this was the first time I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened in terms of after Ambassador Thebault had completed any remarks that he had, what happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Petkovic took the floor and said that he was not willing to talk to anybody below the rank of Halilovic, the Muslim commander in chief. And I didn't want to talk to anybody in this meeting. And I got the impression that he was under heavy stress. So I asked if we could go aside and talk between ourselves, and so we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the conversation you had with General Petkovic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, he maintained that he was -- that Pasalic was far too low rank to deal with Petkovic directly, and he demanded that Halilovic should come to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did you respond to that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I responded saying that we should not allow formalities and protocol to stop us from start working immediately in Mostar, and we should create some sort of organisation for that. And he agreed later on to that, Lasic and Pasalic could start talking to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you make any efforts or did you tell him that any efforts would be made to have General Halilovic arrive in the Mostar region to attend --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I -- I promised that we would do everything to bring Halilovic to -- to Mostar. At the time when I gave this promise I didn't know if I could deliver, but I called Wahlgren to make sure that he was pushed to -- to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the two of you then, General Petkovic and yourself, General, did you then -- the two of you rejoin the larger meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, after that, after the two of you rejoined the meeting, did Mr. Petkovic play any further role in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. It was sort of rather violently interrupted by Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, obviously he claimed that the Muslims had committed some attacks in the area, but it ended with him threatening to kill -- promising that Ejup Ganic would never leave Mostar alive. And then he banged the door and left, and Jadranko Prlic excused him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall how Mr. Stojic was dressed at the time that he --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: As I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- made these statements?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: As I remember, he was in full uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How was he armed if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Sidearm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did he say anything else directed at Mr. Ganic personally, make any statements or --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, it was just this threat that he would not be able to leave Mostar alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can we understand that that essentially brought the meeting to an end?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. Nothing more was said. So we got Ejup Ganic into a Spanish armoured carrier and took him to Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you return after that time to the Spanish Battalion headquarters at Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. We got word that General Morillon and Halilovic were on their way to Medjugorje, so we went up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, in fact, did you speak with General Wahlgren later that evening, again trying to ensure that Mr. Halilovic would be -- General Halilovic would be arriving in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to look, and I hope we'll have better luck than before, if you find Exhibit 1965, P 01965. Sir, this is a report from ECMM dated the 19th of April, 1993. And if I can direct your attention to the bottom of the first page, item number 1 indicates, I believe, "CCO Pol advisor" but you can correct me if I'm wrong, but I take to mean political advisor. And chief of UNMO, Brigade-General Pellnas have accompanied vice-president Ejup Ganic from Zagreb to Mostar for initiation of peace negotiations between Bosnian and Bosnian Muslims. And then over to the next page. At the first meeting in Mostar, attended by the above-mentioned persons and then down through there indicating other persons that were attending. Is this, sir -- appear to you to be a report concerning the meeting that you've just told the Judges about in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. And I would guess that the ECMM presentation or members is probably more correct since they were organising the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know -- this memo's written by someone or at least over the name or from Ole Brix Andersen. Did you know Mr. Brix Andersen?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah, I must have, but I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going back to page number 2, about not quite halfway down the page you will I'll see a paragraph that begins chief of UNMO informed the meeting that the international community and the UN has had all their goodwill used up by the is Serbs and is not prepared to started all over again with the Croats and the Muslims. He demanded that both sides immediately stop fighting before further negotiations take place. Is that at least a fair summary of part of the presentation you made at the time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you then to go over to the top of the third page. And does item number 4 make reference to the intervention, we'll call it, by Mr. Stojic? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Number 4.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There are several references throughout the document to something called the joint operations commission or the establishment of a joint commission. Can you tell the Judges what that meant to you or what you and the other international representatives had in mind in terms of a joint commission?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, the idea was that we would sit together, the UN and the two parties, but also create teams who were also joined by the two parties and a member of the UN or ECMM to go out to the spots where we had problems for the moment. I suppose the name inclined that we had hoped that together we would be able to formulate or even issue directives it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On -- and at paragraph number 5, just briefly it makes reference to setting up or a meeting being anticipated for the following day the 19th of April, at 1000 hours, do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we'll come to that in a moment, perhaps, but is that basically what happened the following day? That there was a meeting.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep, yep, yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you next, please, to look at Exhibit P 01980.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Where do I find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Hopefully you'll -- 1980.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just quickly can I ask you to go to page -- it would be I think the fourth page of the document, to paragraph number 12. And can you just tell us is that again a -- an account or report of the meeting that you attended on the 18th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then take you on, General, to the following day, the 19th of April. Did you make arrangements to travel -- you stayed at the Medjugorje base, I take it.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you made arrangements to travel into Mostar on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who did you travel with on that day, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Together with my adjutant and driver. And there might have been ECMM people coming along as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have other UNMOs from that -- from the Mostar region who were with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Probably Major Ronksley and Grant Finlayson. I can't remember exactly, but they were most certainly with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Paul Ronksley and Grant Finlayson?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Finlayson, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that the first time you had met Mr. Finlayson in person?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to learn that morning that General Petkovic wanted to meet you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I'll pass on that one. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell it us what else that you did then as you moved into Mostar on the 19th of April. What do you recall -- first of all, just setting the screen a bit. What do you recall about the -- what was happening in Mostar at that time? What condition did you find it in? What was happening there?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: We got the definite feeling that the situation was extremely tense, and there were no -- almost no people out in the streets. And why we stayed on one place, ladies came down with tea and asked us in French to "souvez" Mostar, save Mostar. So we felt a bit awkward standing there with no resources. And then we went to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, if I could, to go to Exhibit P 02054. 2054.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, please, what that document is?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It is my report to the force commander summing up my experience in Mostar during the 18th to 23rd of April, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you wrote that report on the 23rd of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you write that report when you were still in Mostar or when you arrived back in Zagreb? If you recall.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe I wrote it immediately after having come back to my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to the -- well, again just for the record if we go to the second page of the document itself, to the top it says "From," and it says "CMO." And does that stand for chief military observer?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Chief military observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that your signature next to that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You give essentially a daily account. Let me ask you to go to the third page and to the 19th of April, 1993. If I can direct your attention back to the second paragraph or -- excuse me, to the second paragraph of that section, the 19th of April. Your report says: "On may way to Mostar I was informed that General Petkovic wanted to see me and I therefore went directly to the ministry of defence. "He stated that he demanded to see Halilovic before any work could start in the Mostar area. He underlined the seriousness in the situation in Vitez, Travnik, and sell notes a." I'm just reading. "he demanded that the focus point should be Central Bosnia, not Mostar." Now, do you recall a meeting with General Petkovic around the 19th of April where these things were said?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, the protocol is correct. There's no doubt about it, or the report is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At this time, if we read through that particular section, you were still making efforts and hoping to have Mr. -- Or excuse me, General Halilovic arrive later that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And toward the end of that -- or at the end of that section before a break in the page it says "He presented General Lasic and his representative." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that what happened at that time when you next had a meeting about the so-called joint commission, it was General Lasic who attended?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you in fact go to a meeting, what might be called an organisational meeting of the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us just briefly what happened at that meeting. Who attend and what happened.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was Brigadier General Pasalic who came over from his headquarters with a number of his bodyguards, and -- but I was -- it wasn't very long until I was called away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to where were you called?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was called to see Stojic, minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall how you received this information, this request?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Probably somebody in the Croatian team got the phone call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you then leave this meeting and go to attend a meeting with Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where did you meet Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: At the defence -- Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: In Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us about the meeting you had with Mr. Stojic at that time? What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, firstly he apologised for his behaviour at the meeting with Ejup Ganic, saying that he had not been able to control himself because Ejup Ganic was such a scoundrel and guilty of so many atrocities. Secondly, he said that they were not willing to talk to anybody below the rank of Halilovic. And he also told me that we should not concentrate on Mostar but, rather, go to other places which were more important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that consistent with the same information, request that you had received from General Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think this was the first occasion when they really pressed the question of the other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any particular reason why they wanted to focus on areas other than Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe they might have been -- the a places they mentioned could be places they were not so well-off militarily at the moment. But that is guess I from my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stojic say anything to you about the negotiations that were then under way with the Muslims about the joint operations commission or any of the other actions or activities that were taking place --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He explained to me that there was little use of negotiating with the Muslims at all because you couldn't trust them anyway. So these were the three messages he sent to me. Start in more important places. You didn't do anything before Halilovic is here, and it would, anyway, be quite useless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going -- going on from that meeting with Mr. Stojic, did you then have any further meetings or did you return to any meetings with Mr. Pasalic and Lasic later that same day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: They -- there was a refusal to work with us before Halilovic came in. So we couldn't get any work done, and I -- I then demanded to see Mate Boban, but he could not be found, as they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall who told you he could not -- well, who did you express your concerns to?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, probably -- probably Pasalic. Could have been Zelenika, but I'm not sure of that. The leader of a Croat delegation, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So at that time, you considered the leaders -- is it correct that the leaders of the Croat delegation at various times would be either Mr. Lasic or Mr. Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I never really got at why they changed, showed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did in fact General Morillon and Mr. -- or General Halilovic arrive later that same day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I got message from Cedric Thornberry, I think, that Halilovic was on his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Thornberry?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was the political head. He was the chief political officer of UNPROFOR at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, we're going to take a break. So it's a quarter to 4.00. We are breaking for 20 minutes, and we shall resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, if we could then come back to this time when, I believe, we left off about the time when General Morillon and Mr. Halilovic arrived. Can you just describe for a moment how it was that they arrived, what the situation was, and what happened after that in the sequence of events?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: As I remember, General Petkovic had come up to the Spanish headquarter and was waiting with us before they arrived, and it was a big entourage around Morillon with journalists, actually, coming down to Medjugorje. But Halilovic was with him, and we immediate -- we starting a meeting there to discuss with the two parties. And the atmosphere was nice and we made concrete results.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did -- in the course of that meeting that you just described, did General Morillon give you the floor at some point, and did you make any presentation or proposal?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I had a proposal that we should immediately separate the two armies from each other. We should create a joint commission, and we should send teams to the trouble spots.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, we're now still talking on the -- this is the 19th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there a further meeting after this back in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: After that we all went down to Mostar, to the Minister of Defence, and Halilovic and Petkovic both made statements about they're willing to create a peaceful situation, and they gave orders to their subordinates to cooperate and to become members of the joint commission and the teams we're going to send out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, just so the record is clear, when you say that there was a meeting at the Ministry of Defence in Mostar, this was the Ministry of Defence of, as you understood it --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. You indicated just a moment ago that at that time both General Petkovic and General Halilovic expressed support for the plan. Did you feel encouraged as a result of this meeting? Did you think that this was actually going to result in substantial change in the local environment at that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think my Scandinavian novice had been crushed before that, so I wasn't too optimistic really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, for the record Scandinavian what --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Novice. I was naive when I came down to this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said it had been crushed before that, so you weren't optimistic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I wasn't too optimistic really. I was very tired because this was late night, and I felt -- I didn't like what I saw, actually. There was a lot of media things around, which was probably nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going then to the next day, the 20th of April, did Mr. Morillon and Mr. Ganic and Mr. Thebault leave Mostar on the morning of the 20th of April for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but I had ask Wahlgren that I wanted to be left back in Mostar, because I thought that all the promises given should be followed up upon a bit. So I stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And later that day was there, in fact, a further meeting of either what was by then or at least in a formative stage what was supposed to be the joint commission?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was at that time Zelenika, who showed up, and Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you talk further about how the joint operations would go forward at that point?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. First we discussed how to separate forces in Mostar and how to get soldiers back to -- to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges whether the concept of a joint police force or joint police patrols played any part in this?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. This was the first time, I think, in the history of Mostar that a joint police force was discussed after the conflict started, and they agreed on that; and, actually, it was created, and I think it lived for 24 hours or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think in one of your accounts, sir, you said you were actually surprised or amazed that the two of them actually -- the two commanders, Zelenika and Pasalic, actually agreed to that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I was a bit surprised, but it was a rather good atmosphere, and I suppose they knew each other from a long time back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I suppose they both had been officers of the Yugoslav National Army. So they had probably met, and we made some progress. I asked them to mark on the maps all the spots they thought we had to handle, and there was a great agreeance about these spots. Only one different; I don't remember which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges what some of the locations were the two of them agreed were the problems areas that needed to be --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was Jablanica, Konjic, and some other village, probably what I have written there, Pasolice [phoen], which is probably Sovice [phoen], and, of course, Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: So we created three teams out of the three other places, and I decided to stay back in Mostar and handle Mostar myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The three teams or these teams that were created to go to these various locations, how were they being composed, or how were they composed?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Major Ronksley was head of one team, and he had with him then a Croatia and a Muslim officer; Grant Finlayson headed the other one; and the third was headed by an ECMM. I think he was a Brit, and I don't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you speak with General Wahlgren -- excuse me, Wahlgren, around this time, about using any element of UNPROFOR, the Spanish Battalion?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. I seeked his consent to be able to bring in as much as possible of the Spanish Battalion, and I told him that I had talked to Morillon about it, and he had agreed. So Wahlgren said, "Go on."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did that seem -- based on your peacekeeping experience in places such as Cyprus and Afghanistan, did that seem to you like a reasonable way forward?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very conventional, peacekeeping method to interpose between the parties to stop them from firing at each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you then make arrangements, in fact -- and let me just say, we'll come back to the joint patrols in a few minutes. But before we do that, did you make efforts then to actually obtain some unit or component from SpaBat and --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- deploy them in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, I was only provided with one platoon, and so I was -- I was transformed to a company commander that day. I had to take action myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record, when we're talking about a platoon in this context, this was a platoon, what might be called a --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Four or five APCs with six or seven soldiers inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And these four or five APCs were then -- armoured personnel carriers were put under your -- put at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: We agreed they should be interposed along Bulevar Revolution, I think the name is. So we took it up position, and we were actually fired at on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this location, the Bulevar, was this a street that ran through Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did you go about actually placing the various APCs then?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: We placed them on positions where they should be able to see each other, but also where we thought there were important buildings. So there would be possibilities to support each other with firearms as they could see each other, which also diminished the length of the area where we interposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sometime after you had deployed the APCs, did you attend a further meeting or have a further communications with the two delegations, the Croat delegation, if you will, and the Muslim or ABiH delegation, about the joint police effort?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I was given the location where the joint police force should be located, and I was also having a promise that I go and see them, so I went there during the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you find when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I found a number of young soldiers, Croat, in the outer room and Muslims in the inner, and there was what I would call a political officer running around there. I met him later on as well. And they were not too eager to do anything, and they had not received any orders to do anything, and I think both parties thought it was too dangerous to go out in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask you about the two groups. You said there was one group, the Croats, in one room, and the Muslims in another room.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did these men appear to you be policemen --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- as we would think of as policemen?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. They were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your reaction to what you saw?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, of course, I thought it was nice that they had been able to get them into the same house, so that was progress; but, otherwise, on that, it was rather disappointing. So I went back to the HVO territorial command headquarters and asked a fellow called Maric to call the two commanders, Lasic and -- or Zelenika and Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Zelenika then respond to --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- to that location?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. They arrived, and I was also a bit agitated because I believe that they had been shot at. We heard -- we heard the noise and gunshot. I really don't know how close it was, but it was enough to make me agitated, so I was a bit rough when we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where in the course of -- when in the course of events that you described in the last few minutes did you believe you had been shot at?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: When we went back from the police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said that Mr. Pasalic and Mr. Zelenika did, in fact, arrive at the location?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said you were pretty unhappy. What did you tell them, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe I threatened to go public with media the next day if they didn't take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was one of the few cards I had to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you think that would make any difference?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I'm is not sure it would have made any difference, but it was the negotiating card I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you get any response from the two officers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. They went on telephone to, obviously, tell people to stop shooting at us, but it was in Serbo-Croatian, so I don't know really what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- well, let me ask you. Were you or any of your people shot at any time later that evening?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did another Spanish Battalion contingent arrive sometime during the evening?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. We got a platoon with carriers with 30-millimetre guns that came up from Split, and we took them directly into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this was, again, a unit of approximately five or six armoured personnel carriers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. It was a rather young captain in command of this, so I put his driver in my car and took him away, and patrolled Mostar during the whole night actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this was in addition to those who were -- which had taken up stationary positions --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. We tried to look impressive with those 30-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was there any conflict or fighting, if you know, in the course of that night?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. On the contrary, it was a rather nice morning the next day. We were extremely tired; but when we got out, people started coming out. So I think the message got around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before going on to the 21st of April - I said a moment ago I would come back to these joint patrols that you sent out under Major Ronksley and Grant Finlayson and the other British officer - what reports did you receive back from the three teams around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Very bad reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: There was absolutely no delegation of authorities to the officers following the teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The delegation of authority to which officers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: To the Croat and the Muslim officers. I think from neither of the sides. They had no instructions, as far as I can see, to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why was that? It may be obvious; but so that there's no doubt, why was that important?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was obvious they had no interest in creating peaceful situation on the spots. On one spot, maybe one side; on another spot, maybe the other. But we got no cooperation. On the other hand, it was very difficult to get through the check-points, and I think it was Major Ronksley at Jablanica who was brought into a meeting where the team was more or less used as a propaganda thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know how they were used --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- in that way?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: They just told me that way. And I don't know if this was this day or late next day, but Grant Finlayson came back and said that he had run into a platoon dressed in black with swastikas on their arms and actually making the Nazi salute. So he was a bit agitated about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had this been in an area somewhere north of Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so. He was on his way to this village, but I don't think he ever reached it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you and the other -- the UNMOs that were working with you, such as Mr. Ronksley and Mr. Finlayson, make any decisions about whether it was worthwhile at that time to continue with these --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I made immediately the decision: Unless we got cooperation, we should not -- we should pull back from these teams and not participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago a report from Mr. Finlayson about a unit, some soldiers in black uniforms. During your time in Mostar in April 1993, did you see any units dressed in black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. We -- there was a special -- I would guess it was a special unit all dressed in black. Very well trained young men with handcuffs on their hips, and under the command of the major in a leather jacket, speaking, in what I remember, an American accent, and this was definitely something special. I tried to find out what it was, and I asked an HVO elderly officer. He was embarrassed, but he didn't want to tell me who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall the location where you saw this unit in black uniform?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah, it was at Hotel Ero.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go forward then to the 21st of April, and were there a meeting between the parties on that day or at least an attempt to have a meeting? Maybe you can tell us whether the meetings took place or not.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it did, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did either Mr. Lasic or Mr. Zelenika attend at least the first meeting on that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was Zelenika, I think. No. No, he didn't. It was this policeman - it's in the report - Filipovic, who appeared instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding how it was that Mr. Filipovic came on the scene, if you will, in the place of Mr. Lasic and Mr. Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. It was a bit astonishing that they did not show up, and I came later to the conclusion that they might have had more important things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you receive any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I heard reports later from people with the UNPROFOR, but they had probably been out preparing for an operation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who I did you understand this Filipovic was? What position or function did he hold in that area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was the chief of police, I understood. If it was in Mostar or the whole of Herceg-Bosna, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he wearing a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you observe about his attitude or behaviour toward moving this effort forward? Mr. Filipovic, I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was not too bad during the first part of the day. I asked them to materialise all their promises to move back their units and so on, and to make sure that the joint police was started to work. I then went for a lunch, and when I -- we started again, I think, at 1800 hours, and then the atmosphere had changed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. How so?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, they -- on the surface, it was good because they produced documents, written documents with orders that the units should withdraw. But the process to -- of the withdrawal showed to be impossible, because Filipovic said that they could not withdraw their units to the barracks until the Muslims had evacuated Hotel Mostar, which was an intolerable situation to have the Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: So I asked -- yeah. So I asked Pasalic why he had not pulled out, and he said it was impossible because of Croat snipers around Hotel Mostar to pull out. Then I asked the Croats to control their snipers, and Maric said they could not possibly control their snipers --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: -- which at the time appeared a bit untrue to me, because most people you saw had mobile phones or other means of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What had been your experience up until that point in time in terms of the -- the chain of command or authority of the HVO officers that you had seen at that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think like in most places in Bosnia the army obeyed orders. They were -- they were controllable. I simply didn't believe the statement that they could not control their snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After Mr. Maric had said that he couldn't control the snipers and, therefore, since the snipers could not be controlled, the ABiH unit could not be taken out of Hotel Mostar --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- what did you do?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was in a moment 22, so I had to do something or give it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, what's moment 22?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Catch 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: So I had to do something or give it up. So I decided to try to do something, and I asked Pasalic, "If I take in a Spanish APC platoon, I'll take your soldiers out." And after some hesitation, he said yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think we will not use the time that we have to go through every aspect of removing the soldiers from -- the Muslim soldiers from the Hotel Mostar; but in the course of the next several hours, on the night of the 20th -- or I believe we're at the 21st --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: 21st, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- 21st, did you, in fact, extract the ABiH soldiers from the Mostar Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, with some difficulties, because it showed up that the platoon I had was the one only with the guns. So there was no place -- I had only one APC and Pasalic said there were 35 people. That would have taken three hours.
