But when we started, a lot of more Muslim soldiers came running in from the surrounding buildings, so there may have been 65 or a hundred of them. But eventually I got a hotel that we could do the job. The only interesting thing is actually that first load of Muslim soldiers were taken into East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: The second load, he refused me to go across the bridge and demanded that we should unload on the western side. That came to be the case. The rest of the soldiers from Hotel Mostar unloaded on the western side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall where -- what location on the west side of the river were they were unloaded?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. No. But rather close to the Bailey bridge, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me go back to --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: But I'm not sure about that. I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go back to a couple of points you mentioned, and take it just a bit slower. You indicated at the time the vehicles that were sent to you or were available to you at that moment, these were essentially gun vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: They didn't have much carrying capacity in terms of passengers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. They were full with the crew already, so there was none in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this limited your ability to evacuate soldiers because you didn't have much carrying capacity --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- in other words.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I had a Red Cross-marked APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's what I'm going to ask you, sir. Before I do that, though, when you left -- when you had had this meeting and you were still at the meeting with Maric, and you were talking about the snipers and what we were talking about a few moments ago, was it was announced at that time -- was there anyone else -- well, was there any other HVO officer at the meeting at that time other than Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think so -- no, no. Filipovic and Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Filipovic, the police chief?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Police chief, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it correct that Mr. Maric and Mr. Filipovic knew that you and Mr. Pasalic were going to the Mostar Hotel for the purpose of extracting the ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let's just cover this couple of points that happened in the course of these events. You did, in fact, wind up using an ambulance -- a vehicle marked as ambulance to remove these soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was the only vehicle available. We were not at war. I had the agreements of the two parties to carry out the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pasalic, General Pasalic, was moving around with you during this time in an effort to get the soldiers, for instance, out of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you at some time in the course of those events put a UN helmet on Mr. Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I put a helmet with a blue clothing on it. If that is a blue helmet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was coloured blue?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Because I wanted to keep him alive until we had evacuated soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the best your knowledge, as a result of that operation, were all of the ABiH soldiers taken out of the Mostar Hotel on the night of the 21st of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, sir: Before we finish on this topic, can you tell the Judges were the -- were all of the ABiH soldiers that you encountered coming out of the hotel were they happy about leaving this location?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: They were extremely unhappy, and we had this what I would call a political fella, who we met in the police headquarters, running around and screaming and telling them not to leave, and we more or less put them into bunches of seven and kicked them down the stairs and into the APC. And I -- I think we were a bit stupid, because we could easily have been shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say "we kicked them," does that --?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: My driver and myself, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was General Pasalic doing?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was rather passive. He was not trying to help us very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But was he giving orders to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Not really. Not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And after you had taken the last soldier out, after you had made the last trip, did you go back with General Pasalic to his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I went with him to his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And where was his headquarters located at that time, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I know -- there was a name on this building, but I don't remember it, but it was on the western side anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that the Vranica building?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you in the course of this it evening, the same evening now, we're still on the night, essentially, the night of the 21st, 22nd of April, after going back to the headquarters with Mr. Pasalic, did you meet later that same night with, again, Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: At the same place as we had -- where we had been before. It was quite -- quite light -- quite late. I guess around midnight sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you report to them or had they otherwise become aware by this time that the ABiH soldiers had been extracted from the Mostar Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, I told Filipovic and Maric that I had carried out my taking away the hinder for them, to go on with bringing their soldiers back to the barracks. And now I -- since I have taken away this obstacle, I really anticipated that they would now do their part of the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the reaction or response that you received from Mr. Filipovic and Mr. Maric when you reported this information?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: A thorough lack of enthusiasm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did understand that? How was that communicated to you?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It wasn't communicated more or less. They were sullen and sour. They were not enthusiastic at all. If I had been expected any sort of praise for what I had done the other night, I was incorrect. So I just anticipated that what I had done was not in their interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How would it not be in their interest?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It seems to me that the obvious conclusion is that they were not too eager to make a peaceful situation in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on to the 22nd of April, 1993. Did you make efforts to meet with Mate Boban that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall to whom you made the effort or made -- try to make the arrangements --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe, it must have been through General Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And through those efforts, were you in fact able to arrange a meeting with Mate Boban at that Spanish Battalion headquarters in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. He came up with his two BMWs and his bodyguards.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where did the two of you meet?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: In the mess, the officers' mess or the canteen, of the Spanish Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Boban and you talk about on the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, I complained bitterly about the lack of cooperation from the Croat side, and I told him about this platoon with swastikas and so on. And he first told me that it was probably the Muslims have provoked, and then I smiled a little and he said that it might have been some individuals who were who were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "it was probably the Muslims who provoked," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He said that it was probably a Muslim unit wearing swastikas to provoke us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you take that answer, his position seriously?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. He noticed that I smiled, so he changed and said that maybe there were some individuals which he could not control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you indicate that you were going to report your experiences and the problems you had with the HVO to the UN in New York?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I made that in rather plain language. The situation got a bit heated for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned earlier this afternoon, when you first met with Mr. Boban in Zagreb at the Intercontinental Hotel, you said that he had made some points to you about a line that he drew approximately between Kiseljak and Vares.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He elaborated on this at this meeting, and it was the idea that they should sort of divide the burden of fighting the Serbs. That he should put his 15.000 soldiers north of the line under Muslim command, and south of the line the Croatian army would be in -- or the HVO would be in full control. So, in practice, what he suggested was a division of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look again at the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Before we move on, can we get an explanation on that? How does subordinating troops divides Bosnia? I know we can cover that on cross-examination, but it would be interesting to get the gentleman's opinion. How does one lead to the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll leave it to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General, I noticed your comment as well. I didn't say anything. But since Mr. Karnavas is on his feet about this, I'll take advantage of it. And can you tell me in what way the deployment of the ABiH and the HVO would have led to a division of Bosnia, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, the power in Bosnia was completely related to the presence of military power, and I have no doubt in my mind that had the Croats been given all military powers south of Kiseljak, Vares, they would have established what was already Herceg-Bosna with the President and the Prime Minister. That is the only logic explanation of what would happen if we had had this share of or division of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to ask you, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Once the ice is broken, it's always dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask another question in relation to this? You told us that Mate Boban said his 15.000 soldiers north of the line, he would abandon to an ABiH command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did he say or do you know or did you know how many Muslim soldiers there were south of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I just add one thing? It is a known fact, and I saw it myself, that in the Tuzla region of responsibility, the Croat units were already rather well entwined with the Muslim forces up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the very points that have been raised is what I was attempting to direct you to, was that if you could go back to your Exhibit P 02054, your report of the 23rd of April.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to page 7 of that report, halfway down the page to the section titled "Meeting with President Mate Boban 1993-4-22."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you look -- scan down that page, sir, and continuing over to the top half of the following page, is that a record of the meeting that you made on the 23rd of April of a meeting that took place just the day before?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you on page 7, toward the last paragraph beginning on that page, it says: "He then came back to the subject he already lectured me upon in Zagreb; namely, the construction of a command system for the military forces. The idea being that Croat forces in Northern Bosnia should be under Muslim control and Muslim forces inside the Vance-Owen Plan areas 8 and 10 should be under Croatia command." Is that consistent with the account that you've just given us in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further -- in further response perhaps the President's question to the Muslim's question, if you go on to the next page, 8, and the second line -- excuse me, second line starting on that page: "I answered that the Muslims obviously fear that his forces in Northern Bosnia could be withdrawn and that the joint command could be closed down."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, just for -- in order to be complete and objective about this, perhaps we could read, at the top of the page, the very first four lines before we go to what his answer might have been, because there we see that what Mate Boban is asking the gentleman is to assist and to -- to assist with Lord Owen in implementing the plans that were already under discussion. Now, of course, we're going to bring this out on cross-examination, but it would appear at least that the gentleman, it seems to me, was ignorant at the time of what the Vance-Owen Peace Plan was all about and what was happening. So if we could read that, because then we glean what exactly Mate Boban had in mind and what his intentions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, number one, Your Honour, there is absolutely no basis to suggest that the ignorance of this man about the Vance-Owen Plan. That's a completely gratuitous remark by Mr. Karnavas. Number two, I assume that everyone in the courtroom could read a couple of lines above, and everyone had the entire document in front of them. Of course, we could read the entire document from page 1 to page -- to the end, if we needed to. But I assume that everyone can read the full context it of the statements, and, of course, Mr. Karnavas can pursue it further in cross-examination, if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You raised with him and you then said: "I briefed him on my experiences in the Mostar area. He was informed that the joint commission with its three teams in the Mostar area not had," probably should be had not, "been able to achieve its goals. This was caused by the unwillingness of the Croat forces to cooperate." Did you feel that when you left your meeting with Mr. Boban that you had pretty much stated your grievances to him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to page 9, last paragraph above the heading that says "Some suggestions." You say -- your report says: "I fear, however, that the question how to give them a decent influence over the Joint Command will be extremely difficult to achieve through negotiations with the Croats. I believe Mr. Boban is dedicated to creating a region in Southern Bosnia where Croats are completely in control. That does not probably mean an ethnically clean area, but surely an area where Muslims are politically and military fully controlled. Process seems already to have started, and will most probably and unfortunately include further fighting and in places atrocities and ethnic cleansing." As a result of the report -- this report was written, you said, when you returned to Zagreb on the 23rd?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me just ask you: Before we move off to other periods of time following your -- this particular mission, can you tell the Chamber then what was your net assessment as you left Mostar on the 22nd or 23rd as to the conditions there, what was happening?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think the lines you just read there capture my feelings. The report reflects also, I think, a bit of, should I say, sadness that we couldn't achieve more, and I left in a very strong feeling that we had a conflict coming. And I told verbally to Wahlgren that I believe we had about a fortnight, three weeks, before it would be a full-scale war, and, unfortunately, I was correct on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the purpose of context, Your Honours, I don't mean to interrupt, but if you could look at the previous two paragraphs. I think that adds context to -- to the portion that the Prosecution read. I think it's important that we see things in context as the gentleman recalled them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we go on, as of the time you left Mostar, had you seen any indications that the joint police force was -- was working or had any chance of working at that time in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't even know if -- if it still existed when I left Mostar. I doubt that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall that right around the time that you left Mostar that there was some legislation passed that you've mentioned in one of your accounts about the status of refugees in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I think about the same day as we left, there was a decision taken not to allow refugee Muslims to stay in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me then direct your attention forward to a meeting in Zagreb on the 30th of April, 1993. Did you have a meeting with various parties on that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. Owen and Vance were in Zagreb, and I was summoned up by Brigadier Wilson, who asked me to come and present some sort of solution for creating a joint military force between the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was General Wilson?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was my predecessor, as chief military observer, and had left for work as military advisor with the ICFY, International Conference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you remember who attended this meeting in Zagreb on the 30th of April for the HVO or Bosnian Croats side?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. General Petkovic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you present any proposals during this meeting about a possible organised joint operation or Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I suggested a Joint Command and under it a joint territorial army and two small units or two units of national army or national guards, and it was deliberately put in a way what you could interpret it in many ways. You could have a big territorial joint army, and a very small National Guard. So you could have a rather small national territorial unit and rather big national armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was constructed to get an acceptance on the idea of a Joint Command and a joint territorial thing, because if you could have them join forces over the territory, it could probably stop them from killing each other, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir - you said General Petkovic was at this meeting - what his response or position was or participation in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I believe, he said on one occasion that he saw there is little possibilities to form a joint -- a Joint Command together with the Muslims. But my main impression was that he was absent-minded and not very interested in what was going on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on what? What did you see or observe that caused you to think that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was not very active in the conversation. I got the distinct feeling that he was not very interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you said a few moments ago, in fact, the fighting then did break out in Mostar just, as you said, about a fortnight later, on the 9th of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall receiving reports from UNMOs and UNPROFOR, in fact, on the 9th and 10th of May, describing what was happening in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I ordered the Mostar team to report directly to me about the events in Mostar those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look at Exhibit, in your binder, P 02276.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is an UNPROFOR report dated the 10th of May, 1993, titled or subject "Mostar situation." And going to the body of the report on the second page, does that give a -- essentially a chronology of events from approximately 5.00 that morning until midnight on the 9th?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A number of these entries, for example, the entry at 1530, and about halfway down as one example, it says: "UNMO reports ten buses carrying men, women, and children; left football stadium; and heading towards Citluk. Stadium is now empty of civilians." When you say "UNMO reports," is that indicative of the fact that the UNMOs in the Mostar region were sending these reports to you and UNPROFOR around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go next to Exhibit 2269. Sir, this appears to be an UNPROFOR report dated the -- again, the 10th of May, 1993. And if we go to the second page, up in the upper-left corner, I think -- can you see 2HQ UNPROFOR Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I'm on the wrong paper. 22?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't have that paper. Maybe here it is it. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you can turn to the second page, there's a cover -- essentially a cover page, but there's a bunch of stamps on it?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the second page, it says, towards the upper right -- excuse me upper left corn, it says, "Headquarters, UNPROFOR Zagreb." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In one of the boxes below that, again, listing number -- listing various units or organisations, do you see "HQ UNMO"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to turn to the next page of the document, which is numbered page 2 in the upper right corner, in item C, Southern BH command, item 1 Mostar, again, does this reflect information that you began to receive on the 10th of May, 1993, as what was happening in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Toward the end of the paragraph, that numbered paragraph 1, it says, "HVO check-points have been set up to deny movement in to and out of the city. The SpaBat company has withdrawn from the city and is keeping it under surveillance." Did you come to know around this time that UNPROFOR and the international organisations were being denied access into Mostar around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me next ask you to turn please to Exhibit P 10008. That would be toward the back, I imagine. It's a big number. P 0 -- three 0s. I'm sorry, P 10008. I think, sir, it will be pretty much -- it will be toward the back of the bundle.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry. Yes. Okay. Say again, please.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, this appears to be a memorandum or a communication dated the 10th of May, 1993, from Wahlgren, UNPROFOR Zagreb, to Annan, UN, New York. I take it Annan is Kofi Annan?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this makes reference to a meeting with Radic, the Chief of Staff for the President's office, and Susak on the 10th of May, 1993. And Mr. -- or General Wahlgren reports in the second sentence of that paragraph number 1: "I was accompanied by DCM Pellnas and Abdul Aziz." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you just confirm to the Judges that you did, in fact, attend the meeting with Mr. Radic and Mr. Susak?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when it says Mr. Radic was the Chief of Staff, President's office, he was the Chief of Staff to which president?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: President Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you said -- or Wahlgren says: "I was accompanied by DCM." Do you recall who DCM was? Well, first of all, what that stands for, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: All these abbreviations. Deputy chief of mission. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall who it was that also was with you that day, besides General Wahlgren and Mr. Abdul Aziz, if you recall? If you don't --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Should have been -- no, I don't remember. It should have been Cedric Thornberry, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Toward the end of that paragraph, on page 1, the first section on page 1, you, again, indicate: "UNPROFOR was being prevented by the HVO from having access into the city, making it difficult to assess the situation there." Was that on the 10th of May, 1993, and did that continue throughout, really, the balance of 1993, the summer and fall of 1993, to be one of the major international concerns?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't remember when we were first let back into the town. It took quite a long time, I believe, before UN could enter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Scott. I am a bit puzzled because I thought this was the document from Mr. Wahlgren, but you refer to it and you say, "you state that" to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I did, I misspoke, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I thought there was something that I had misunderstood. Line 10 on page 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At any rate, Your Honour, if I did, I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The report, sir -- the document indicates what I had read to you and this is general -- just so the record is clear and so there is no confusion, this is General Whalgren's report; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise if I misspoke. In the -- about the middle of that paragraph, it said, "I stated," "I stated," I'm quoting, Your Honour, "I stated that ECMM were reporting that Croatian army forces were moving towards Mostar." Do you recall what other information either you or UNPROFOR or General Wahlgren had on that -- at that time about the involvement or movements of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't recall. One has to go back to documents and reports to be sure. I -- I don't have it in my head any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to page number 2, item 2, section 2, Radic referred to Tudjman's message to President Izetbegovic and Boban, a copy of which is attached. And while we're at this point, if I could then just ask you keep your finger, if you can, at this exhibit, but would you also look at P 02265.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please. And this appears to indeed be a letter from President Tudjman dated that day, the 10th of May, 1993, to Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban. And do you recall whether it was Mr. Radic or Mr. Susak, one of those gentlemen in the meeting, that presented to -- to the -- let's just say, the UN delegation, General Wahlgren, yourself, the others, a copy of President Tudjman's letter?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go back to the memorandum of the meeting with Radic and Susak, again, toward the end of paragraph numbered 2, on the second page, it says: "Susak suggested that UNPROFOR should contact Boban directly and express the Croatian government's readiness to exert some influence on him to cooperate. He said that he personally would guarantee access of the people being taken out of the city." Did -- do you recall whether Mr. Susak explained how it was that he would personally guarantee --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- access to the people in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could next ask you to go to Exhibit 2254.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, correct. 2254.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a note by the president of the Security Council, again, dated the 10th of May, 1993. Let me direct your attention in particular to the second page, top of the second page. It says: "The Security Council calls upon the Republic of Croatia in accordance with the commitments under the Zagreb agreement of 25 April 1993, which is (S/25659), to exert all its influence on the Bosnian Croat leadership and paramilitary units with a view to ceasing immediately their attacks, particularly in the area -- areas of Mostar, Jablanica, and Dreznica." Do you recall at that time what the relationship was between the Croatian government and the Bosnian Croat leadership?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't think there were any problems between the two parties at that time. As I said earlier, it was generally known that everybody thought in UNPROFOR that Susak had a special amount of influence in the Herceg-Bosna region. But how the political lines were going and who was commanding what, I don't, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Wahlgren and the others that were part of the UN delegation that met with Susak and Radic on this very same day, the 10th of May, 1993, did they have this Resolution in hand or -- excuse me, note by the president of the Security Council in hand at the time they met with Susak?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: They might at least have had the text, I guess, which they could have had on beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. General, I want to move forward then to the summer -- we're leaving the 9th and 10th of May for a moment, and if we can move into 1993. I would just like to show you some of the reports that you were receiving during that time period. Could I ask you, first of all, to go to Exhibit P 03094; in other words, 3094.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: You say 03?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Maybe they haven't been -- okay. 3094. If you have that, you'll be there.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. 3094. I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pellnas, this is a letter from the acting senior military observer from BiH south, Medjugorje, on the 1st of July, 1993, addressed to Lasic; and in the second paragraph, it starts: "I also find it rather curious." Mr. Rosenroll indicates that they are still -- they're not having any access in to Mostar as of, again, the 1st of July, 1993. I think you said a few moments ago, there was a lack of absence into Mostar for a substantial period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. A lack of presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did that affect the ability -- I mean, again, for the record, so you -- how did that affect the ability of the UNMOs to do their job?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, we could not report what was going on inside Mostar, for sure, and that was the effect of it. Not exact what you could notice from a distance then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to next go to Exhibit - and I'll try not to confuse you - just 3148. This appears to be a report from UNMO -- an UNMO report dated the 3rd of July, 1993. And, again, if I can just direct your attention quickly to section -- it's under "General situation" in item B: "BH south: Mostar access still denied ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to go to the fourth page of the -- that exhibit, to the bottom of that page under -- under heading D, "Meetings." And BH south reports contacted "HVO LO," I submit is liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: " ... regards restriction of movement, and in particular the inability -- inability of MXA to return to Jablanica. LO stated he had passed our concerns on to higher authority and would forward their reply when it was forthcoming." Do you recall any further information about who that BH south was dealing with at the time as the liaison officer, and what more senior authorities were involved in this?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look at Exhibit 3376.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this appears to be an UNMO report dated the 10th of July, 1993, and on the second page under, again, section B --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Hang on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. "BH south."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you see that again: "Mostar: Access again denied"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me just look at a few of these, and I will probably discard a few for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interest of time, I will skip over some of these, but with the understanding that we will submit them by motion or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go, sir, to the next -- next to 4464.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have an UNMO in the area around -- in August of 19 -- 1993, excuse me, named, if you recall - and he realise you may not recall all these names - but Dan Ashitey?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. There were over 500 coming and going, so I don't remember many names, unless I really bumped into them and talked it them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to go to the second page of this report, toward the bottom of the second page, it says: "Discussion, General Petkovic/Captain Collingwood. In negotiations with UNMO requirements, the following points were required by UNMOs from the HVO." The first one mentions a police escort. Then going on to the next page, number 2, "Access/ability for UNMOs to cross front line north of Buna." And, again, this is dated, I should say, to put this in context, this is the 25th of August, 1993. 3, "Access to Mostar by any route (HVO controlled) at all times." And then we can see points 4 and point 5. And then in the next paragraph, we get the responses to the various five points. And if I can ask you to look in particular about four lines down in that section, it says, "Item 3," which is, "Access to Mostar by any route." "Item 3 was acknowledged although it was questioned and not well-received." Did you receive any other information from the UNMOs under your command around this time, what the nature of the continuing objection was to granting access to the UNMOs was?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Further into that paragraph, "When asked how long UNMOs expected to remain in Mostar, I replied," again I'm quoting, I being presumably Ashitey?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "That it was our intention to remain until the cease-fire completely breaks down. To this, General Petkovic replied that we should not ask for HVO help to get out, if the cease-fire breaks." And do you know if, in fact, the UNMOs got any greater access to Mostar, in fact, around this time, late August 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't remember. To see that, one has to check with reports coming in later, I think, to see what happened actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just show you the next exhibit, 4785, primarily because I want to ask you about a topic that's only come up once or twice, and if you can shed any light on it. This is another UNMO report dated the 3rd of September, 1993, from BiH south, paragraph under "Operations," paragraph B, "Patrols, MX5," which I think the Chamber knows is the UNMO -- the designation or the call-sign for the UNMO team in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It talks about apparently 7 to 8.000 refugees in Blagaj. Let me ask you though, specifically, to go to the next page, item F and item G. Did you understand, during this time, that one of things that both UNPROFOR and UNMOs were attempting to monitor, in addition to other things, was aircraft, the movement of aircraft in the airspace of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. I don't think that the air observers on the ground took a special interest in aircraft; but I suppose if they saw them, they would report on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For example, under section F, it gives the report. The report's coming from an ABiH brigade in Blagaj, but it's reporting the use of aircraft by HVO to drop some sort of clusters, it says, of 120-millimetre mortar bombs. Do you know whether there was, apart from international flights, whether there was a no-fly zone in Bosnia-Herzegovina during this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I would have to go back to papers to see what no-fly zones indicated at that time. So I pass on at that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Item G, "Other," references air drops. "Aircraft still dropping pallets too far into the east into Serb territory. BiH forces report no aid reaching areas north and south of Mostar. These areas require aid as much as main Mostar." And it's suggesting some various map coordinates are listed there for the purposes of the air drops. What do you recall about the international community's efforts to air drop relief supplies into the Mostar area around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I remember that there were air drops; and, obviously, reading this, they were as uncontrolled as all this -- or inaccurate, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go next to 5085, an UNMO report dated the 15th of September, 1993. And if I can ask you to go to the -- physically turn to the fourth page of the document. And, again, in the --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Which I don't have. I have page 3 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If you go to what's marked as page 5, and item G, "Other," and the only part of the document I'll take the time to ask you about at this point is the paragraph that says: "BH informed the UNMOs that cease-fire agreement has been reached between BH and Croatia. Apparent --" excuse me, "agreement to take effect 18 September. Apparently, 79th cease-fire recorded and success unlikely. It was confirmed that agreement was with Croatia and not BH Croats." And let me just ask you, sir, if we can get your general -- your reaction here to -- does that sound to you about right, that by September of 1993 there had been something like 79 cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: If not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your, not only your personal, but the other internationals that you were also working with, how did you feel about the situation when the cease-fire was announced during these times?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, after a while, in these conditions, you -- you don't take much notice of paperworks or oral statements. You wait to see what happens. So you don't get, I would say, optimistic or pessimistic about the announcement that a cease-fire has been signed. You wait and see what happens before you make any valuation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, do you have a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Croatia isn't mentioned anywhere in the Croatian translation, but the Croatian Defence Council. Now, an agreement was never written between the -- between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was always the BH army and the Croatian Defence Council, if it was an agreement and in the Croatian text. So it just says "Croatia," so can we clear that point up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, only the -- sir, if you still have that item in front of you, item G, "the 79th cease-fire," does the UNMO report state: "It was confirmed that agreement was with Croatia and not BH Croats"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I have no comment on it regarding what was just said. It may well be incorrect in this paper. It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to Exhibit 5127.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under BH south, again, "Mostar. Unstable. Thirteen impacts fired directly at team Mostar east accommodation from 20-millimetre anti-aircraft by HVO this morning. Verbal and written protests lodged. Firing stopped when team Mostar West went to Mostar OZ," operational zone, "to complain." Can you tell the Judges what sorts of reporting were you receiving from UNMOs in the Mostar region about their personal situations during this time, the summer and fall of 1993, in terms of sniping or shelling?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was at the time very skeptic about having the observers inside the town at all because it was rather dangerous. So it is always a decision to make, whether it makes -- whether the risk is worth taking. And as it turned out, we decided to stay, but I was not completely in control of this. The BH command also had a great say in where to locate the observers, even move than I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, because some of these abbreviations might become confusing. When you say "BH command," you're talking about UNPROFOR command?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exhibit 5234. UNMO report from the 20th September 1993. Item number 1, "General situation. Medjugorje calm. Mostar, unrelenting bombardment of East Mostar since 0600 hours today. Hundreds of artillery, tank, and mortar rounds. UNMOs on the east bank have had to bureau deep into their bunker." It says, "HVO explains bombardment as punishment for BiH attack on Hum hill. Did you recall -- I mean, other than this one, do recall other reports from your UNMO teams, from the Mostar region, that some of this shelling will take place as some sort of punishment or payback for something that had happened in the area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: There was a constant rather heavy shelling going on, and I don't remember that it was related to punishment or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think, finally, on this one, and perhaps the final one before the break - I think we're coming up on about the time for the break - 5519. And this is an UNMO report from the -- covering the period the 29th of September to 30th of September. And I just want to ask you, specifically, on the last -- no, I'm sorry, not the -- the next to last page. On that page, on item number 6, again, aircraft sightings, and it makes reference to the times coincided with airdrop times. What was the point of -- what was the point of your UNMO officers reporting this information about aircraft sightings? Why was that part of their report, I guess, is the point?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, I think they would report anything they would think was of any significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under SMO assessment, SMO is senior military observer?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In item 8: "The situation remains calm. However, although we cannot say there is a build-up, there is a lot of movement and activity around the AOR."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Area of responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "Denial of access over the past two days supports speculation the HV are operating in the region north of Neum." Do you recall any particular reports or information you were receiving around the end of September, 1993, about HV operations in that area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't especially recall. When you read one report now, you may see paragraphs which you think are remarkable, but it was a steady flow of reports on all corners of the former Yugoslavia, and we might have well at this time been pretty heavy occupied with problems in Mostar for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this, because hopefully we'll come back to this topic before we finish your testimony. Is that something the UNMOs were looking at or trying to be aware of on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it seldom happened that they had to report an aircraft passing and so on; and, secondly, I think they normally were not, I should say, focused on these sort of things. We had this no fly organisation with special teams placed at the airports and checking what was going up and down. We had observers at the Zagreb airport, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the -- my final question, perhaps, before the break is the second topic that I raised under this: What about the topic or subject of HV movements, the Croatian army movements or involvement, is that something that the UNMOs were attentive to or reporting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. They would report immediately if there were HV movement inside Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why was that something deemed important or reportable?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, that would have been an intrusion by Croatia into another acknowledged country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that might be the time for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pellnas, I'd like to move now to the end of 1993, to approximately December. First of all, let me just ask you how you became involved, and we might work backwards just a little bit, so you can tell us the context, as you recall it, for the request for you to become involved in a particular effort. In December 1993, were you asked by Lord Owen to become involved in negotiations, again, in Mostar concerning something called the -- that was being proposed as the European Union Administration of the City of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. He sent me out there to -- there was an agreement between the parties in Bosnia. He sent me out to "delineate," as he said, the area that would be administrated by the EU, and that was all the guidance he gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's start when you said -- so there's no misunderstanding, when you said there was an agreement between the parties in Bosnia, there was agreement as to how the EU --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: That's EU should administer this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So in concept?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you sent then into Mostar again to -- in an effort to do that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. It was very strange mission because as you know the fighting was still going on in Mostar and I was sent there to make the parties agree on how to delineate the area for the EU.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know -- do you have any recollection of approximately when this concept of an EU administration of Mostar kind of as a UN -- or EU, excuse me, protectorate, when that concept first began to be discussed?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had there been any discussion around this time about who might serve as the EU administrator of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: The I think the first rumours had come up when I started that it was Mr. Koschnick from Bremen who was the German candidate for the job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to look to Exhibit 5757. First of all, let me ask you if we can just again set the context a bit more. As of the time that you got involved several months later, when you arrived in Mostar in January 1994, what was the position of the Croat side that you first encountered when you arrived in Mostar in January? What was their position as to the delineation or administration of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was headed by a lawyer by the name Tomic, and when we started to discuss the delineation of Mostar, he produced the idea that the EU would administer -- should administer East Mostar and nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was that consistent with what you understood the EU concept or mandate to be?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, the EU should -- the idea was to maintain a multi-cultural Mostar with the entire city under the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now if we go then back to 5757, this appears to be a letter from Mate Boban dated the 8th of October, 1993. And if you look at the last page, it's being addressed to particularly Owen and Stoltenberg, but also European Community foreign affairs ministers. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, the -- the letter goes on for some pages talking about why Mostar is a Croat city, and if anyone wants to argue with me about that, everyone can read the letter, and the Judges can read the letter. But if you can find -- if you go to page number 3, to the middle of the page --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second paragraph beginning on that page which says, "In all types," and at the end of that paragraph Mr. Boban says, the conclusion of the last preceding sentence: "The Croats only have Mostar. Therefore, the Western European Union request is absurd." And is that reflective of the position or posture that you encountered when you arrived in Mostar in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, before answering that question. I object to the form of the question. How can this gentleman possibly comment with respect to what Mate Boban is saying in this letter about the absurdity of what the Western governments think versus what Mr. Tomic, I believe, the lawyer, was advocating. Perhaps if there was more testimony, it might assist but I think it's best to take the testimony from the witness as far as what he heard, what he learned in great detail, as opposed to pointing to a letter and saying, does this comport with Tomic's position, because I think Mr. Boban is speaking about something in a much broader context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think my question was a proper one and the witness was there on the ground in -- in January and February, and I think he can say -- he can say for himself whether this sort of -- this sort of feeling, this sort of position as depicted in this letter are similar to the positions that he encountered himself during those negotiations. It's a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we get a ruling, Your Honour? Can we get a ruling first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott, I'm trying to understand what you're getting at and what you would like the witness to express. There is a sentence on page 3, and so you would like the witness -- you would like to ask the witness whether what is said here in the sentence is indeed what he saw, what he learnt while on the ground. Is that the idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, not just that particular sentence, Your Honour. If we want to spend the next 15 minutes reading the entire letter from the beginning to end we can do that. It seemed to me that's not necessary when everyone in the courtroom has the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Scott, the problem is that he doesn't know the letter himself. I mean, he did not know the letter then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was whether what is depicted in this letter, which he can read as well as -- or better than many of us, is that the same -- essentially, the same or similar posture that he encountered when he arrived on the ground in January, February, 1994. And he can clearly say, "Yes, this is basically what I -- the same posture or attitude that I encountered at the time."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again Mr. President, Mr. Boban is speaking about other matters in a much broader sense. The gentleman was there at a meeting. He met with Mr. Tomic, and I believe that later on he met with Mr. Buntic, and then I believe there was also another meeting with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Buntic was there, although Buntic didn't say anything. Perhaps it would be better to get the information from the gentleman. He was there. What did he observe, what did he hear, what was learned? Then if the Prosecution feels the need to go back because they want to, somehow, get the gentleman to say, "Yes, this letter comports with what I heard," perhaps there would be sufficient foundation, but at this point in time the gentleman is being asked to divine into what Mr. Boban was thinking at the time when he wrote the letter -- well, that's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, with due respect, I understand this differently. We read what Mr. Boban wrote, and the witness has spoken to several people in Mostar about Mostar and the future of Mostar, and the question is whether these other people told him the same thing, whether the essence of what all the others told them corresponds to what is written in the letter. I think that's a legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If indeed it is a legitimate question, then I would, with all respect, suggest that perhaps we hear from the witness -- from the witness all the meetings with respect to this particular issue, because he needs to get in Mr. Buntic, who agrees, and then Mr. Tomic again, who apparently goes back. So I think, perhaps, if we hear it all it might be better in order to understand, but I leave it -- I'll leave it up to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please then, Mr. Scott, can you please ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pellnas, you've heard the question I put to you several times now. If it will help make it -- if it will help give you some further context and orientation on the letter, because I know the use of the police in Mostar was something that you were interested in all -- for a long time, including back in April 1993, so let me, before I put a further question to you, go back to the first paragraph of Mr. Boban's letter and it says: "Following the Western European Union 5 October 1993 statement about the initiation of planning for a possible police deployment as support forces of the reputed European Community planned protectorate of Mostar, allow me to stipulate the position of the Croat party in relation to this issue." Again, when you look at this letter and the claims to Mostar and everything that's in here, the demographics, everything that everyone in the courtroom has in front of them and can read, is this similar to the attitude and positions that you encountered, voiced by the Bosnian Croat representatives in your negotiations in January, February 1994?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: As far as comes to what Tomic said during negotiations, I think he fairly well reflected these opinions about Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know who made Mr. Tomic the head of the Bosnian Croat delegation for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. I anticipated that it should have been Mate Boban, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn before leaving Zagreb to go once again to Mostar for the purposes of these negotiations who would be leading the Croat team, the Bosnian Croat team or delegation, if you will?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I learnt that a certain Mr. Tomic will lead the Croat delegation. We had no information at the time who was going to lead the Muslim delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you heard about Mr. Tomic being involved in this capacity, did you have some information or basis for being concerned about your future dealings with Mr. Tomic and how productive that might be?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, I got information, and I don't remember from whom, that he was a hard-liner and absolutely dedicated to Mate Boban. So I got a bit worried about the prospects.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What did you do based on those concerns?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I went to see Mr. Sarinic in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who was Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was chief of Croatian security with Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did you say to Mr. Sarinic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I raised my fear that I would run into problems, and he then assured me that I would have no problem and Tomic would be very reasonable and he was not in the pocket of Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn anything around this time as to what Mr. Boban's status or position was in the Herceg-Bosna or HVO government?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Up till the moment when the federation became a political reality, I think he had a very strong position, but after that he -- he was an obstacle to the future more than a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know what position or role he was given after he was removed as president of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He was the -- he was -- became the president of the Croatian petrol company INA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where was that company, that petroleum oil company, based?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was based in Zagreb, so he had his there, and he stayed most of the time at the Intercont.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The Intercontinental Hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And so you'd received these assurance that is Mr. Tomic would not be a problem and then when did you -- what do you recall arriving in Mostar then?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I don't remember the date now. It may be in the paper somewhere. It's -- I went up to the Spanish Battalion, and they were not too happy to see me because they haven't heard about it. So we called General Briquemont who was the commander-in-chief in Bosnia and he was also very irritated because he had not been informed, and he ordered the Spanish Battalion to house me and -- but to give me no further assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just stop so the record is clear before we go too much further. I notice that in the transcript the reporter has made a note at line 20 that INA, I-N-A, and I think there won't be any dispute with the name, that is the name of the oil company that Mr. -- or General Pellnas was referring to, I-N-A?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: That should be capital letters, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So once you arrived in Mostar or Medjugorje and were -- found yourself a place to stay, did you see Grant Finlayson again?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that the atmosphere in the Spanish Battalion headquarter was not likely to produce a cup of coffee, so I called my observers and asked them to take me out. So they gave me transport and took care of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: And I had to, because we had no information about the Muslim delegation. There was none. So I had to decide to go into Mostar and try to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Mostar, I believe you said -- or Medjugorje, and correct me, please, you stayed in a hotel during this time, I think?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I stayed in the hotel Ana Marija in Medjugorje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And did you check into the hotel sometime that day?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did during the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you encounter anyone that you had met before in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Jadranko Prlic was there with an entourage of, I think, three -- maybe two or three people in leather jackets, and with all the normal insignias what goes with leather jackets in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Meaning?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Meaning gold rings and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have a conversation or exchange words with Mr. Prlic at this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He came up and said hello, and quite ironically asked if I was going there -- if I had come to create peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you seen -- in your time in the former Yugoslavia, had you encountered other, as you said, men that were dressed in this way?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: On many places, not least Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Doing what?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: In -- they were most of the time in -- in the business, that is, smuggling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- perhaps the gentleman should -- should be asked to quote from his book, because he's referring to Montenegrin politicians who are smugglers. So that's the context of the book, and I think it goes into the state of mind of the individual as to what he thinks of the people in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think that's an excellent question for cross-examination, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, if he's -- if the gentleman -- if the Prosecution is going to go into it -- if the Prosecution is going to go into some of it, he should go into it completely, but the reason they don't is because they know that we have limited time for cross-examination, and that's my dilemma. You see, if I had enough adequate time for cross-examination, then I would -- which would be two or three days for this gentleman, then obviously I can go into those at my leisure. But I think if they're going to touch into it, have him exactly describe and he should tell us, what does he mean by Montenegrin politicians as being smugglers of the type that Mr. Prlic looked like or his "entourage" looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: In addition to that perhaps Mr. Scott can refresh all our recollections as which paragraphs of the indictment deal with the wearing of leather jackets and why we're taking up time with this. It's just another example of trying to assassinate characters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't make up the witness's evidence. The witness encounters Mr. Prlic in his hotel, and he exchanges a couple of -- a few words with him and he simply says this is how I found them. I think that's simply reporting direct eyewitness observation. And that's all it is, and if Mr. Karnavas wants to go into it more on cross-examination then he's certainly welcome to do so if he thinks it will assist him to go into it further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I fail to understand, Mr. Scott, is about the leather jacket question. I mean, in what way is this important or relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Chamber -- you'll have to -- ultimately have to decide that based on the totality of the evidence in the case and that's all I can say, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, can you please proceed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you then go back into Mostar either later that day from the hotel or the following day to begin these actual negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I went into Mostar the following day as I remember, and the observers brought me in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say the observers, you mean Mr. Finlayson and the others?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. But also a team that was already in Mostar met us because they had an armoured car.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I just want to spend a few minutes on your actual travel into Mostar on this occasion. Can you tell the Judges a bit about the route that you followed, what you had to do to actually gain access into the city of Mostar, into the centre of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: As I remember, there was only one bridge left where you can come over to the eastern side, and we used that one which I think is south -- or was south of Mostar. And then coming up to an area as I remember could have been a railway area. There were some containers, and we had to pass fro and to a couple of times before we got into a road that led us into the centre of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once you then began into East Mostar -- travelling into East Mostar, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was shocked by what I saw because I hadn't been there since the events in April 1993, and there was no way what I would recollect or recognise anything in East Mostar to what I seen before. It was only the mosque or the remnants of the mosque that were made an orientation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do I understand, sir, that the conditions in Mostar and the physical condition of the city was substantially worse than what it was when you were there in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I would say that it was considerably worse than in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when you moved into -- when you travelled into the city, and before we -- getting to the point where you make this particular observations now, can you tell the Judges whether your vehicle -- your vehicle or the UNMO vehicles that you were travelling with at the time were shot at at the way -- as you entered into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Not when we went into Mostar, but when we left Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. When you arrived --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: A young British --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry go ahead?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: -- a young British officer, who drove them, he had -- he had some ideas where snipers were located up on the hillside. So he was a bit worried about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, did you say -- then we will come back to that in a few moments. Now, you said you indicated a few moments ago - excuse me - that you were going into Mostar in part to arrange -- to meet with the Muslims about organising a delegation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On that date, did you meet with someone named Klaric?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I met with him in his office. He -- to the best of my knowledge, he was the mayor of East -- so-called mayor of East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did Mr. Klaric have a deputy by the name of Alija --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Alikadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Alikadic. Sorry for my pronunciation. But that's the man that you knew?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: After meeting, first, with his deputy, did you have a meeting with Mr. Klaric himself?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us a bit about that meeting, the impression that Mr. Klaric made on you, and what he said to you in terms of negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He made a very good impression on me because he was very controlled. He was probably dressed and washed and shaven, which nobody else around him was. So he made quite a distinction from his surrounding. So I was impressed by that. He was also very cool. When shells landed rather near, he didn't blink. He was very, very controlled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was about to ask you, in fact, was there shelling going on of Mostar around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. Around every fifth minute, a few rounds landed. I thought it was 12-centimetre mortar shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did that continue around throughout the time that you were meeting with will Klaric?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it did. He started by accusing us that the UN, European Union, were letting them down and not protecting them. So he was quite aggressive in the beginning, but later on he promised to -- to put together a team and send it up to Medjugorje later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then when you left the meeting with Mr. Klaric, where did you go? What route did you take?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: We went the same way back; and then in this, what I recall as a railway area, we were shot at from the hillside. And we had, on the second, I think, three impacts in the car; and on the last round, we had a number of impacts, one hitting the window where Grant Finlayson sat. But it was small calibre rounds, 7.62, so it made no harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall did the meetings then between the two delegations, that is, the Bosnian Croat delegation and the Bosnian Muslim delegation, begin sometime after that? I don't know exactly what the passage of time was, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think it was maybe a week or something before we could get the parties together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this first meeting went, and can you confirm, in fact, was it this Mr. Tomic who appeared representing the Croat side?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. And as I said, his only concept was -- with the European Union was to administrate East Mostar, and that was not quite the idea we had about it. And so I went out and telephoned Sarinic in Zagreb and told him that I thought I was using up my young life for nothing and -- in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you were able to get -- this was the same Mr. Sarinic that you had talked to in December?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the security advisor to Mr. Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you have an understanding of what happened next?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, Tomic was suddenly called to the telephone, and when he came back he was furious and said I was negotiating behind his back, and it appeared that it was Mr. Susak who had called him. What he has told him, I don't know, but he was furious.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: How did you learn or what information did you come to have that it was Susak who had recalled Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure who told me. Could have been the telephone people with the Spanish Battalion or more probably Tomic himself, because he was just furious. But I remember it clearly because it was a bit odd. I called Sarinic, and it is Susak that calls back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And even after that intervention, did anything come of the meeting? Was any progress made in that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
