utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at Exhibit 7584? And this is an ECMM report of the 14th of January, 1994. If I can ask you to look to the paragraph titled on the first page"A, Political Situation."

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it is correct, the interpretation. I mean, I was sent out with almost no mandate at all and no guidance and under the circumstances where the parties were still fighting. So I suppose you could say that Lord Owen used me as a sort of guinea pig to see what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And down further in that paragraph, number 1, do you see the reference, in fact, to the meetings under "the chairmanship of General Pellnas"?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant was rather correct. It was rather insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But that is a reference to the meetings that you were beginning to engage in around this time?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any meeting with this General Lasic, the same Lasic that you had met with in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. I had him in rather good memory, actually, so I invited him for dinner Medjugorje, also with the idea that I would try to create a better atmosphere for negotiating, and asked him to stop shelling Mostar while we were negotiating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what response did you get from him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, we had some wine, so he was in good mood and promised, but the next morning he called back and said that it wasn't possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your assessment of him saying the next morning that what he committed to the night before was not possible?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I think he had probably be come under pressure or he just regretted what he had promised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was your response to that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I told him that I would haunt him down to hell, if he didn't stay by his word. That was probably the correct words. And it appeared later on that he actually did, or it might have been a coincidence, but the number of shells during the time significantly diminished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us a bit more of an idea of that specific idea? How --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Just a few rounds hit Mostar during the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During those three days?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And compared to?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Three hundred a day maybe. So I like to think that he kept his word.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going forward in the course of negotiations, and I'm trying to -- some of these things you've already touched upon, so I'm trying to not to repeat them too much again. But when you say later that there were other meetings where you, then, ultimately made some proposal as to what the map should look like.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. Since nobody came up with it, I had to draw map myself and present it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what did that map -- I mean, very broadly, just in concept, how did you propose that the city would be --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: The first map was Mostar in itself and as little as possible outside the city, because I didn't want the EU administration to have borders to the Serbs, which would have created another problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how was that -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: And, as I remember, the airport was not included in the first draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did the two sides receive your proposal?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Tomic put it in his briefcase without any comments, just saying that he would give it to his superiors who they might have been. And the Muslims said, well, maybe, yes, perhaps could be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did there come a time when these negotiations moved to a meeting in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Must have been -- could have been February, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And who attended, in terms of the senior, if you will, representatives of the two parties?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I was to form a small group in which this Mr. Buntic mentioned here before turned up as the negotiator for the Croats about the delineation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: And he agreed to my proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did Mr. -- Excuse me, were Mr. Izetbegovic, Mr. Tudjman also involved?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. They -- they were there, yes. But this -- I did not deal with them. I was on this level dealing just with the concrete question of delineation of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And had you met this Mr. Buntic before?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I'd never seen him before. And then I called in the Muslim delegation and said, "We have an agreement."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: And they said, "No. We don't have an agreement because we need the airport."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I -- leading again to a stalemate. Is that --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. So it was -- it appeared that at this time the Muslims had no interest of receiving a quick solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you have any -- can you provide the Judges any insight or information as to why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah. It is, of course, also an evaluation of a situation, but I believe that they had military success in the enclaves further north, and they were in no hurry to settle the Mostar business at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In February --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you please to look at Exhibit 7965?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just come back to this last answer. General, is that your appreciation of the situation? So it's a bit of a speculation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, like all political judgements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In 7965, this is an ECMM report for the period covering the 19th of February to the 25th of February, 1994; and I think if you look down into the text it, you'll see your name, and do you agree that this is a report largely upon the status of the negotiations concerning the EU administration?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Which page do I appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: 7965. I think in the first paragraph. First page, first paragraph, number 1.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "This hot issue has been dealt with by the Mostar administration working group chaired by General Pellnas." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. Yeah. One may perhaps smell a bit of organisational envy here, but I don't know. On the whole it is correct. It was not very relevant for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, the next bulleted the paragraph, it starts: "CRHB representatives consider that such an administration should be restricted to the town and the airport should not be included in it. None commonplace of all CRHB politicians is the capitality of Mostar." And is that consistent with the positions you, indeed, encountered in your negotiations?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you go to the top of the next page, please. I asked you earlier about what Mr. Boban's status was, and the man named Pogarcic apparently says or had given the information that he was on an extended vacation in Croatia. Nobody knows when he will return. By this time, the latter part of February 1994, did you have any more information as to what Mr. Boban's status was?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to Exhibit 7904?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you look at that and tell us what that is, because it's addressed to you.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep. I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the record, tell the Judges what this is.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It is a letter from Klaric, in short, saying that they will not -- due do what is happening in East Mostar, they have decided to cancel their representation in the further negotiating. They will not attend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so that it's clear, you understand this to be the same Mr. Klaric that you had met with a few days earlier?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look next at Exhibit 8019.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This appears to be the report of a delegation that went to Mostar in March of 1994. It's dated on the top of the first page Geneva, 25 March 1994. On the bottom somebody named Elmar Dinter.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know if you can shed any light on who Mr. Dinter --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Dinter was the liaison officer from the CMM at the ICFY in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the persons, this is addressed to ICFY, and your name seems to be listed in the second line?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It's a whole -- it's the whole ICFY headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then on the second page, this appears to indicate that around this time there had been a -- a French delegation -- a kind of joint French-Spanish delegation to Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And it gives a report of the mission. The third -- excuse me, the fourth overall page of document, if you start with the first page, and the fourth physical page starts. It says, "Trip report on the European Union administration of Mostar." And it appears, do you agree, that the letter gives them a synopsis of meetings with various people in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I had no information at the time about this trip and about this combined friend. I don't want comment on it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you about the content of the document. For example, on page 3, when it says, "Mr. Klaric expressed a few principles on the European administration of Mostar." He says, "Mostar must be an open city. Mostar cannot be a part of the territory of the CRHB. Mostar cannot be the capital of CRHB. All refugees must return to their homes." Is that consistent what you understood Mr. Klaric's position to be during the times you talked to him?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But as a matter of fact, I did not talk so much with Klaric, except for the first meeting. It was his deputy that made the negotiating?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that was Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Alikadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- Alikadic. And did he, Mr. Alikadic, express --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: He had the same ideas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you recall as a result of your meetings around this time you continued -- you came back from Geneva. We've talked about that before we went to the exhibits, and this is where this Mr. Buntic appeared for the first time. Did you have another meeting back in the Mostar-Medjugorje area after Geneva?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I had this meeting where only the Croatian delegation showed up and the Muslims stayed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did Mr. Buntic appear at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, and I was promised that it should be led by Mr. Buntic, but the fact is that he did not say a word during this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who -- who led the Croat delegation?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: It was Mr. Tomic. And as a fact he went back on everything they had accepted in -- in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the end of that meeting, sir, can you just told us was there -- had there -- was there any resolution in sight or had there ultimately been any progress on the agreement between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. We were back at square one. Both parties had abandoned what they had agreed on. I had agreement from both parties but never at the same time. And what -- it was my impression that Mr. Buntic obviously was more closely connected to Zagreb, and Tomic was not, actually. He might have had other interests. I saw him at the time as the spokesman for Mate Boban. But that is also a guesswork from my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, around this time then after the end of February -- or around the end of February, actually, 1994, did you understand that the Washington Agreement came into effect and the federation, the Muslim-Croat federation, was established --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- at least on paper?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And were there negotiations then in Brussels concerning, again, still the topic of the EU administration of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes. It was led by the Greek ambassador, because Greece had the chairmanship of European Union at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was an --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: But Michael Steiner from Germany played a very important role.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was an EU administration ultimately put in place in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, finally we got to the agreement about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know approximately -- can you tell the Judges approximately how long that administration lasted?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Now I don't know how long it lasted. For quite a while, actually. Long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was this Mr. Koschnick in fact appointed the administrator from Bremen?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, but we went in there with his should I say, Chief of Staff or deputy, on a beforehand mission at what time we met Mr. Zubak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And let me just ask you before coming to that: Is this -- were you, once again, after the Washington Agreement and after Mr. Koschnick was essentially named the administrator sent back once again into Mostar to try to lay further groundwork?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you accompany --

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: After Geneva, I didn't deal with Mostar except from the fact that I followed Ambassador Metsher into Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that was my question to you. Was there a time when you went with ambassador, the German ambassador, Metsher, into Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this period within the indictment? If not, if not; meanwhile it might be interesting and I would like to discuss this matter over a beer with the gentleman, perhaps this is not the best forum to have discussions on matters that are outside the scope of the indictment and the period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour, because the period of the indictment, it goes to at least April of 1994, and I thought the Chamber would, frankly, want to know a little bit about not the end of the story but at least the end of this chapter of the story about the administration of Mostar, after all the things that the Chamber's heard about from 1991 forward. I have about -- several -- three or four questions left on the topic at all. And it is -- but in any event, the bottom line is it's within the period of the indictment, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As long as it's within the period, and if he wishes to go outside the period, as long as we're able to go into the period so I can discuss Mr. Prlic's involvement at Dayton and thereafter, I don't have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I've already said it several times, this is within the period of the indictment we're talking -- that we're now -- so I think it is more than reasonable to at least finish this part of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said you went with the German ambassador Metsher. Was this part of an EU advance party?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did this trip into Mostar compare to the trips into Mostar that you made before?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Well, the agreement made -- the fighting had stopped so there was no hostilities in Mostar at the time, nothing really.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know during the time that you continued to be involved either in February, during the January-February period - and, sorry, in the interests of time -- because of time I skipped over it - or again in this later period were you still pushing the idea of a joint police -- some sort of a policing agreement for Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No. This idea had been taken over by the European Union. It was a great discussing matter in Brussels, but I was not involved in that matter. I just intervened in the negotiation by telling Michael Steiner that they had to have very strong wordings in any document dealing with a joint police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And why did you give that counsel?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: I had my background and my misgivings about the possibility to create a joint police force. I thought it would be a very superficial organisation and the communities would continue to work business as usual below that surface. But I was not involved in the direct negotiation about the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you accompanied Mr. -- Ambassador Metsher back into Mostar at this time, was that the last time that you were in Mostar during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I can change to a different topic and the last topic of direct examination. I asked you earlier in reference to one of the reports that I showed you whether the UN military observers were regularly interested in the possible involvement of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you understand that as the chief UNMO, if you will, to be something that was part of your mandate and the UNMOs' mandate, among other things, to monitor?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you to go to Exhibit 785.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Sorry. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This appears to be a report from the senior military observer of BH south dated the 20th of November, 1992. "Subject: Special report on presence of CA troops in Herzegovina." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, at the time what did you understand the abbreviation "CA" to be?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Croatian army, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there is a reference in the second numbered paragraph to information that was being received about the presence of a number of numbered Croatian army units. If you see that paragraph. The 1st, 4th 145th, 116th, 162nd, parts of the 2nd and 3rd Brigade with a total of 10.000 to 12.000 troops. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for clarification purposes, in the continuation of the sentence it say that the mentioned units were put up in the region of Konavle, and Konavle is in the Republic of Croatia. It's an area in the Republic of Croatia. That's what I wanted to explain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in reference to paragraph numbered 1, General Pellnas, do you recall any information that was received in connection with General Petkovic around this time of the involvement of the Croatian army in the Stolac area?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In item number 3 on the third page, it says,"Assessment: Brigadier Petkovic's statement prove the independent presence of Croatian army fully under their own command." And then making reference to a Colonel Grubac, "detailed information." Do you recall what other steps that the UN military observers, around this time, the end of November 1992 took to -- seeking to verify this information?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't think they were out seeking information. They patrolled on what they saw. They reported. I don't think they were -- but this is also an assessment. I don't know. I don't think they were especially running around looking for HV units. But when they come -- came across them, they probably reported. I have one comment on this paper which --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: -- perhaps should be made. I believe this Colonel Grubac is a Serb officer. So one should be a bit careful about what is reported here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise once again, but just another clarification. I think it will be easier for us to clear it up straight away. This document relates to the actions of the Croatian army for the liberation of the southern parts of Croatia, and that is why the document refers to the Serb army or Serb officers and the Croatian army is also mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, again that's counsel testifying, and they can put evidence on that if they wish. And the fact that it's a Serb -- this is a Serb source of information is said right on the face of paragraph number 1. "During my meetings with Serb authorities," which -- I mean I think everyone can read that, if it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you said a few moments ago though, or earlier today, this afternoon, that the presence of Croatian army units in Bosnia-Herzegovina was something that was important and something UNMOs were interested in, I mean, that concerned -- had continued back even before your time. That was something the UN was always interested in; correct?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 205. This is Security Council Resolution 752, dated the 15th of May, 1992. And if I can direct your attention to paragraphs number 3 and 4 on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gentleman was not in theatre at the time, so he's being asked to comment about something at a period of time when he was not working as an UNMO. If I understand him correctly, it was from November 1992 to November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The testimony of the witness, Your Honour, was that this was something -- this was an issue that the UN military observers was -- were continuously interested in. There is a reason they were interested in it, because of UN Security Council Resolutions, and this simply provides the further foundation for what the witness said, that this was part of the responsibility of the UN military observers to monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question is did military observers exist at the time, and was this observed by military observers at the time. In other words, did this information that the Security Council put in, in the resolution, did that come from military observers? If it did not, if it did not, then I suggest that this is not the right gentleman to be asking these sorts of questions. So I think some background information might be necessary, assuming the gentleman can answer the question. He was the chief military observer. Perhaps he could tell us as of what period of time, when exactly did the military observers, the UN military observers arrive in theatre. And if they arrived after this particular date then, obviously, this gentleman is not competent to answer any questions regarding this resolution, and I suggest that the Prosecution bring over whoever it was that drafted this, who provided this information to the UN and as a result that information got into the resolution itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as a UN military observer, I take it you worked -- a UN military observer worked for the UN?

utterances.speaker: BO PELLNAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the Security Council is part - I think we can all agree - it is part of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question, again, I'm asking for clarification. First, we need to establish as of when. The fact that -- this is a UN tribunal. Does that mean that because a UN tribunal, everything that the UN does is correct? Come on. This is the whole point of having this exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- if I can respond, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Scott, you want to respond. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not sure why Mr. Karnavas is so exercised about this. These are officially UN records that anyone can access. I don't think there's anything, doubt -- they have been fabricated in some way. This man worked -- he was the chief UN military observer during this time period from November of 1992 to November of 1993. He's already confirmed to us several times that part of his mandate was to monitor these things, and this is simply part of the UN official basis for him being involved in these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Here is the problem that I'm having with this. The document can come in through somebody else. But now the gentleman is asking to vouch, to vouch for the authenticity, the reliability, the credibility, or the truthfulness of what's contained in the documents themselves. That's what is, in essence, he's being called upon. And I think the gentleman wasn't there. UN military observers weren't there at the time. So if the document -- if the Prosecution wishes to get the document in through some other witness, they can do so. But to have this gentleman somehow vouch for what's in the document itself, and it appears that is what is happening. I think the Prosecution made its point, and that is that one of the things is at that period of time, while he was there, they were looking for Croatian army involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that point was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you were the chief of the United Nations Military Observers; and when you took up your position, were you aware of that there had been resolutions passed by the UN Security Council?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have here in front us a resolution that dates back to earlier than your arrival in theatre. Were you aware of this resolution dated 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Very well. In this resolution that you were made aware of, at paragraphs 3 and 4, interference from outside is mentioned by units of the JNA and elements of the Croatian army, and the UN Security Council demands that this stops immediately. What we see at paragraph 3 and 4, does that reflect the situation you became familiar with when you took up your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was one of the reasons, of course, why United Nations observers should and must report every observation that the Serb army or the Croatian army appeared inside Bosnia. There were also many other things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just stated something that could be extremely relevant. You said that the United Nations Military Observers had to observe what was going on, including the presence of the Serb army or the Croatian army. Were you given specific directions or instructions in that respect, or did you yourself and the people working with you improvise in that respect, or was this part and parcel of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was part and parcel of our mandate, but I can't recall that I had specific written instructions. We could all read the Security Council resolutions and see how they affected our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Scott, then, could you please resume. This was only a technical problem in order to have the question put without raising objections that are a waste of time. But, unfortunately, I think we're going to have to adjourn, but you can finish this topic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't be able to finish. I think I will need tomorrow, and I think I'm still just barely at three hours. I think I would need, approximately, a half an hour or so in the morning to finish. And I would remind the Chamber that it's the only witness we have this week, so I can't imagine why we are going to be short on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll discuss this among each other, among the other Judges when we meet tomorrow morning. This additional half hour, of course, we also have to provide the Defence with additional time, of course. It's five after 7.00. We will now adjourn and will meet tomorrow, but remember the hearing is tomorrow in the morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 6th day of June, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.03 p.m.,
